## Findings by module

### 8

- **confirmed** (ch-006 (Chapter 1, development and underdevelopment)): Rodney defines underdevelopment as comparative and as a relationship of exploitation (two answers: the imperialist system bears major responsibility; Africans must understand and overthrow it), uses a Marxist stage scheme (communalism, slavery, feudalism, capitalism, socialism), and uses 1960s data (per capita income, steel, calories, doctors). This is the position the course's Module 8 labels 'Rodney: the trade underdeveloped Africa [debated]'. Present as one position and one framework; note that the stage scheme is Marx's and was already contested, and that data here are 1965-68 snapshots, not pre-colonial evidence.
- **confirmed** (ch-009 chunk 1 (Chapter 4, numbers)): Rodney says estimates ran from a few million to over a hundred million and cites a recent study of about ten million Africans landed alive (Curtin, 1969, not named in the passage), which he treats as a low figure, and puts Middle Passage mortality at 15 to 20 per cent. The Voyages-based figures in the course (about 12.5 million embarked, about 10.7 million disembarked, roughly one in seven lost) agree with Rodney's ten million landed and a Middle Passage loss of that order: our arithmetic, 12.5 minus 10.7 is 1.8 million, 14 per cent. Good worked example of why a 1972 estimate and the modern database can both be quoted if source and date are named; Rodney's argument that records understate smuggling is a caveat, not a number. Diop's 100 to 300 million (Precolonial Black Africa) is in the range Rodney calls speculative.
- **refined** (ch-009 chunk 1 (Chapter 4, Arab and European slave trades; gold to slaves)): Rodney insists on calling it the 'European slave trade' for Atlantic exports and argues the East African ('Arab') trade also served European plantations (Mauritius, Reunion, Seychelles, cloves of Zanzibar). Course Module 8 'other slave trades' names trans-Saharan and Indian Ocean flows. He also says the Gold Coast shifted from gold to slaves 1700-1710 (5,000-6,000 captives a year) once Brazilian gold was found: dates and numbers are his secondary sources; a good case of switching export mix. Apply with care: the capture-as-violence argument is his, and he accepts that rulers acquiesced from self-interest.
- **contradicted** (ch-007 chunk 1 (Chapter 2, slavery in Africa)): Rodney claims that in Africa 'there were few slaves and certainly no epoch of slavery', that captives in communal societies rapidly became ordinary members, and that most slaves were in North African and Muslim societies. Course Module 3 (Almoravids, Ahmad Baba's opinion), Module 4 (Songhai) and Module 8 ('other slave trades') show slavery in the Sahel and Indian Ocean worlds; Diop's Precolonial Black Africa gives Songhai slave estates. Present Rodney's claim as a position; the evidence in the other books shows large-scale slavery in some states (not 'a mode of production' everywhere). Work: tag [CONTESTED].
- **contradicted** (ch-008 chunk 1 (Chapter 3, 'Europe decided')): Rodney writes that Europe fixed what Africa exported and that Africans 'had little clue' about the system; Thornton (named in the course, not ingested here) argues Africans controlled the terms on the coast and the trade rested on African demand for goods and political power. This is the live disagreement the course already records: Rodney, Manning, Nunn on one side; Thornton on the other. Present it with Rodney's own examples of African refusal (Kongo, Dahomey), which show limits to the 'decided by Europe' claim. Tag the long-run effects [CONTESTED].
- **contradicted** (ch-008 chunk 2 (Chapter 3, causes of the trade)): Rodney says Europeans enslaved Africans for economic reasons and racism came after as rationalisation, and that 'Africa helped develop Europe in the same proportion as Europe underdeveloped Africa'. The proportion claim has no measure and is rhetorical; the course should avoid repeating it and keep the Voyages numbers as the only quantified claim. The racism-after-economics sequence is argued, not shown. Tag as one position.
- **contradicted** (ch-009 chunk 1 (Chapter 4, population, maize and cassava)): Rodney states population stagnation had 'no causative factor other than the trade in slaves', which Manning (named in the course) tests with demographic models and finds partly different; the claim is contested, tag it. He also rejects 'slave trade apologists': he says maize and cassava became staples in Africa late in the 19th century, from the Americas, and that this would have occurred without slavery. This contradicts Diop's claim (Precolonial Black Africa, ch. 9) that maize and cassava reached Africa before Columbus; two books in this set conflict. Choose Rodney's account (American origin, later spread), which matches mainstream Columbian-exchange history (outside these books); and note his late-19th-century 'staples' date is later than other work on their spread.
- **contradicted** (ch-009 chunk 5 (Chapter 4, anti-slavery and imperialism)): Rodney argues anti-slavery was a pretext for colonisation, citing British action against Jaja and Nana (who by then traded palm oil) and Leopold II's forced labour. Course Module 8 lesson 3 (abolition, legitimate commerce, road to Berlin) can present this as the 'pretext' reading beside the humanitarian reading; these cases (Jaja of Opobo, Nana of Itsekiri) are not in the course and their dates are not given in the text. Tag as one interpretation.
- **contradicted** (ch-009 chunk 6 (Chapter 4, 'pre-colonial' as preparation)): Rodney concludes that the first four centuries of Afro-European trade 'represent the roots of African underdevelopment' and that 'pre-colonial trade proved to be a preparatory stage for colonial rule'; and that colonisation succeeded because of African 'weakness'. Course Module 8 lesson 3 'testing the label pre-colonial' notes the label can imply that the Atlantic age was only a prelude to colonialism. Rodney's usage is the very teleology the course warns against; present it as his argument and the reason for the warning, not as a neutral label.
- **extended** (ch-008 chunk 1 (Chapter 3, African resistance and the 'Europe decided' thesis)): Rodney's case that Europe took the initiative and set Africa's role: Portuguese seizure of Ceuta (1415), forts on the Gold Coast, firearms and cloth for captives, 'Europeans selected what Africa exported', and a table of African resistance: Matamba under Nzinga (founded c.1630, Portugal gained the upper hand 1648, trade resumed 1656), Baga leader Tomba (c.1720) defeated, Dahomey's Agaja stopping the trade 1724-26 and resuming in 1730, and Benin's reluctance to sell males. Course Module 8 lesson 2 names African agency and limits with Thornton; these are concrete cases for it. The dates and details are Rodney's summary of secondary work; the Estaban Montejo 'scarlet' quote is a recollection by one Cuban ex-slave, which Rodney himself calls poetic, not evidence of mechanisms.
- **extended** (ch-008 chunk 2 (Chapter 3, Africa's contribution to European capitalism)): Rodney's Williams-style thesis: gold, slave-grown produce and ports (Liverpool, Bristol, Nantes, Bordeaux) fed European capital accumulation (Barclays, Lloyds, Watt's steam engine), the 'guinea' coin (1663) named for Gold Coast gold, and racism as a product of slavery. Course Module 8 weighs the debate; the Williams thesis is itself contested by later historians (outside these books, not verified here), so present it as Rodney's position built on Williams (1944), not as settled. Specific claims (Barclays' 1756 slave trade, Watt's debt to West Indian owners) are secondary-source assertions I cannot check here.
- **extended** (ch-009 chunk 2 (Chapter 4, technology and requests for skills)): Rodney's 'technological arrest' argument: African cloth was exported by Europeans (Benin, Yorubaland, Senegambia, Loango) before cheap imports displaced it; the Dahomean saying that whoever makes the powder wins the war; requests for skilled craftsmen rather than ships by Lebna Dengel of Ethiopia (Portuguese embassy 1520), Agaja Trudo (1720s), Opoku Ware (1720-50), a Calabar king and Adandozan (c.1804); the Axim ban on Ivory Coast canoes after 1637 as an example of cutting inter-African trade. Course Module 8 lesson 2 can use these as concrete cases of African agency within limits. His claim that iron smelting was abandoned because of trade is contested; the dates for each request are secondary-source dates I could not check.
- **extended** (ch-009 chunk 6 (Chapter 4, Scramble, compradors, Berlin)): Rodney argues the Scramble came from European competition (spheres of influence breaking down once one power imposed tariffs), that racism confirmed direct rule, that African agents (Senegal's four communes, Gold Coast coastal troops, Luanda/Benguela communities, Sierra Leone returnees) made conquest easy, and that political fragmentation was the weakness Europe exploited; also African attempts at reform before conquest (Gezo's palm-oil edict of 1850, Glele, Gungunhana, Muhammad Ali, Merina schooling). Course Module 8 lessons 3-4 (Berlin myth: the conference did not partition Africa) can add the 'Scramble as competitive chain reaction' reading, but Rodney does not discuss the General Act itself; so the correction of the Berlin Conference myth is not in this book. Text says 'fourteenth century' where the context is the nineteenth: an error in the edition.
- **note** (ch-003 and ch-005 (Preface, Introduction by Harding, Hill and Strickland)): Rodney states his purpose: understanding present African underdevelopment, with limits fixed at the 15th century and the end of colonial rule, and arguing that development needs a radical break with the international capitalist system (Preface, Dar es Salaam). The 1981 introduction by colleagues is a biography (Rodney b. 13/03/1942, killed 13/06/1980 in Guyana; book first published 1972 by Bogle-L'Ouverture and Tanzanian Publishing House). It quotes his two-level answer: imperialism bears major responsibility, and Africans bear responsibility for understanding and overthrowing it. Use only to label the book as an explicitly political, Marxist work by a Guyanese historian, 'one position', as the course does in Module 8.
- **note** (ch-007 chunk 5 (Chapter 2, conclusion)): Rodney concludes most African societies before 1500 were 'transitional' between communalism and feudalism, had no epoch of slavery as a mode of production, no internal social revolutions, and a 'slight edge' for Europe in 1500; he quotes a Dutch description of Benin (streets 120 feet wide, king's palace the size of Haarlem) as evidence of comparable development. The Benin quotation is from a 17th-century Dutch compilation (Dapper) and cannot be checked here; treat it as a European description, not an African source. This is a clear statement of Rodney's pre-colonial baseline for Module 8: it frames the Atlantic encounter and is itself argued, not measured.
- **note** (ch-010 chunk 1 (Chapter 5, colonial wages and trading companies)): Chapter 5 begins the colonial-period analysis: low African wages (Enugu miner 1 shilling a day; Gold Coast European civil servants 40 pounds a month against 4 pounds for Africans), South African and Congo mining profits, Kenyan land alienation, Firestone in Liberia, and trading companies (CFAO, SCOA, UAC) whose capital partly came from the slave trade. Out of scope for this course (after 1885); one useful link for Module 8: Rodney traces Bordeaux and Liverpool slave-trade capital into palm-oil and groundnut trading, the 'legitimate commerce' transition. The wage and profit figures are unchecked.
- **note** (ch-012 (Postscript by A. M. Babu)): Babu's 1971 postscript from Tanzania: development needs a break with production for the world market, foreign investment is a cause not a cure, and North Korea and Albania are praised as examples. It shows the book's 1970s policy context (Tanzanian socialism, dependency theory); these policy claims are outside the course period and have not aged well, so cite only to date the book's politics.

### 5

- **refined** (ch-007 chunk 1 (Chapter 2, culture and Ife/Benin)): Rodney says the Ife and Benin bronzes 'date from the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries', as evidence of development before European contact. Course Module 5 dates Ife naturalistic heads to roughly the 12th to 15th centuries and Benin's brass-caster plaques to the 16th and 17th. The two differ for Benin; Rodney's single span is loose and was written in 1972. Keep the course's tagged ranges; use Rodney as an example of a 1970s generalisation that compresses two traditions. Also notable: he prefers 'cultures' to 'civilizations', and says religion in pre-colonial Africa both mobilised states and slowed technical change.
- **refined** (ch-009 chunk 3 (Chapter 4, Ibadan and the selling of captives)): Rodney says Ibadan sold its own captives and serfs for firearms and so undermined its base, and that European slave buyers made the decisive difference. The argument rests on a Marxist reading of serfdom versus slavery; other historians stress internal Yoruba warfare after Oyo's collapse. Present as one interpretation; the 100,000 population of Ibadan, Abeokuta and Ajaye is a mid-19th-century estimate by visitors.
- **extended** (ch-009 chunk 3 (Chapter 4, Oyo, Asante, Dahomey)): Rodney's regional cases: Oyo as an inland cloth-and-cavalry empire largely outside slave exporting until the late 18th century, exporting captives in numbers from the early 19th, and falling by about 1830 (successor states Ibadan, Abeokuta, Ijebu, Ajaye); Asante absorbing captives locally (Odonko-ba descendants of captives); Dahomey as the 'black Sparta', a tribute-paying part of Oyo until Oyo's fall, with militarised politics. Course Module 5 lesson 3 compares these three; use Rodney's contrasts (inland versus coastal, labour retained versus exported, despotism versus council) as comparison rows, tagged as his reading. Ife/Benin bronzes: he says the earliest were best and quality declined from the 16th to 18th century, which is an art-historical judgement, not a date.

### 2

- **contradicted** (ch-007 chunk 3 (Chapter 2, Kush and Aksum)): Rodney says Kush's decline in the 4th century CE was 'completed by attacks from the then expanding Axum' and that Axum was founded by a Sabaean-origin dynasty in the first century CE. Course Module 2 tags 'Aksum destroyed Meroe' [CONTESTED] (Ezana's inscription mentions a campaign against Nubian peoples, with trade shifts and environment as other factors) and gives Aksum c.1st-7th century. Keep the course's tag; show Rodney as stating the contested theory as fact (1972). He also says the Zagwe (12th century) claimed descent from Moses and that Solomonic kings replaced them in 1270: agrees with the course's 1270 date.

### 1

- **contradicted** (ch-007 chunk 3 (Chapter 2, diffusion of iron and brass)): Rodney says West African brass casting 'is generally held' to have come from Egypt via Kush, with brasswork similar to Meroe's, and that Kush was a source of iron-working for the continent; elsewhere he says iron arrived in most of Africa after the birth of Christ. Course Module 1 lesson 3 tags the independence of West African iron [CONTESTED] and notes the radiocarbon plateau; Igbo-Ukwu bronze (Module 5) is dated around the 9th century and has a local tradition. Rodney's diffusionist line (Kush as source) is one side; show both. His 1972 date for iron 'after Christ' is later than Module 1's first-millennium-BCE evidence.

### 3

- **extended** (ch-007 chunk 3-4 (Chapter 2, silent trade, trans-Saharan trade)): Rodney calls Bovill's silent-trade account of Ghana's gold 'dumb' and says it is a rough approximation of first exchanges and not a permanent procedure; the people of Bambuk and Boure were in regular trade by Ghana's time and Mali ruled them. He adds: trans-Saharan capital came from Maghrib merchants (Fez, Tlemcen) who sent agents south, so the trade was partly a colonial-type relationship; the Sudan exported few slaves (Kanem-Bornu raided the south for captives); Ghana took Awdaghust c. end of 10th century; Taghaza held by Songhai against Morocco; Mandinga/Dioula traders used scales and brass weights (benda). This is a third view on silent trade (Olivier: Mali's traders did it; Diop: peripheral peoples; Rodney: not permanent). Show all three and state the safe wording: reported by Herodotus and Arabic authors for peripheral peoples, not a general method.

### 7

- **refined** (ch-009 chunk 5 (Chapter 4, Shaka and the mfecane)): Rodney explains Shaka's innovations (short stabbing assegai, discarded sandals, impi 'horns' and chest, reserves, regiments up to age forty, a standing army of 30,000) as outgrowths of Dingiswayo's age-regiment system and a growing population squeezing clan segmentation, with Zulu rule free of slave trading; he treats Nguni movements as state-building. Course Module 7 lesson 3 tags the attribution of these innovations to Shaka alone [CONTESTED] and lesson 4 weighs the mfecane debate. Rodney's account stresses collective origins and is consistent with the cautious course wording; his army size and 12,000 square mile figures are unchecked and the Mfecane is not questioned here (written before the 1980s critiques the course cites).
- **contradicted** (ch-007 chunk 4 (Chapter 2, Zimbabwe)): Rodney dates the Zimbabwe stone buildings to the 11th to 14th centuries, says the 11th-14th century builders were 'believed' Sotho-speaking and that a Shona-speaking Rozwi dynasty set up Mutapa in the 15th century (first Mwene Mutapa 1415 to 1450), and claims Great Zimbabwe was Mutapa's first capital. Course Module 7 gives Great Zimbabwe c. 12th to 15th centuries built by ancestors of the Shona, Mutapa emerging in the 15th (traditional date), and Rozvi/Torwa as later states. Rodney's Sotho builders and Rozwi-founded Mutapa conflate later states and are older scholarship; trust the course. Rodney agrees on the key point: the builders were Africans and the Rhodes-era assumption of white builders is false.
- **contradicted** (ch-009 chunk 4 (Chapter 4, Zulu dates)): Rodney gives Shaka's birth about 1787, headship of the Zulu clan 1816, death 1828, and the Zulu defeat of the British at Isandhlwana in 1876. The battle was fought on 22/01/1879 (outside these books; the course's Module 7 Zulu lesson should carry the correct date; the course dump gives no Isandhlwana date to compare). Treat Rodney's 1876 as an error and do not cite it; Shaka's dates (about 1787 to 1828) are traditional dates, [TRADITIONAL DATE]. He also says Zulu territory grew a hundredfold from a 100 square mile clan base, an unverified figure.

### 6

- **confirmed** (ch-007 chunk 4 (Chapter 2, interlacustrine zone)): Rodney discusses Bunyoro-Kitara and the Bachwezi (long-horned cattle, barkcloth, earthworks at Bigo with ditches over six and a half miles), Engaruka's terraced iron-age settlement before 1000 CE, banana agriculture, and treats the Bachwezi as a product of African synthesis, as with Aryan and Dravidian in India. Matches Module 6 lesson 3 (Ntusi, Bigo, Chwezi tradition [CONTESTED]). He says oral traditions 'imply kingdoms' before the Bachwezi; the course keeps the extent of the empire contested. The Bigo ditch length (about 6.5 miles in the book) differs from any figure in the course: do not quote.
- **confirmed** (ch-008 chunk 1 (Chapter 3, Kongo and Afonso)): Rodney says the king of Kongo in the early 16th century objected to the slave trade, had asked Portugal for masons, priests, clerks and physicians, and was swamped by slave ships. Matches course Module 6 lesson 4 (Afonso I's letters; Portuguese trade). Rodney's phrasing 'forced him to specialise' is an interpretation; the letters show Afonso also taking part in slaving. Use the course's letter-based version and show Rodney's summary as the underdevelopment reading of the same source.
- **confirmed** (ch-009 chunk 4 (Chapter 4, interlacustrine states, Hamitic myth)): Rodney says Europeans invented the thesis that Great Lakes states were built by white 'Hamites' from Ethiopia, that even if the Bachwezi came from Ethiopia they would be black or brown Africans, and that they took the local Bantu language; Babito (Luo) successors from the 16th century; Buganda dominant by the 18th century with barkcloth and an appointed-district administration; Rwanda with ubuhake cattle clientship, Tutsi/Hutu/Twa as castes and classes, Mwami Rujugira and Gahindiro. This supports Module 6 outcome 'Reject a racial theory of state origins' and lesson 3 (Buganda). Rwanda's Tutsi/Hutu/Twa description uses 1970s stereotypes of physique; do not repeat the diet-and-height explanation (our judgement).

### 4

- **extended** (ch-009 chunk 5 (Chapter 4, Sokoto, Samori and the 'gale-force wind' image)): Rodney lists Sokoto, Ahmadu, al-Hajj Umar and Samori Toure as 19th-century state builders, the Luba-Lunda complex, Merina kingdom; and uses the image that Africa entered slave trading 'as into a gale-force wind' that shipwrecked a few societies, slowed many and left African captains making decisions until about 1885. A useful hinge for Module 4 lesson 4 (Sokoto) and Module 8; the metaphor states the middle position of the Rodney-Thornton debate and is his own. Also: he rejects Senghor's 'bush fire' image.
